LinkedIn posting is regular but (B4): "LinkedIn posts get lovely comments and roughly zero bookings." The single highest-converting visibility play on record is one guest podcast: (F4) "one guest spot on The Standup Log podcast brought four clients in a fortnight, which taught me borrowed audiences beat building my own from scratch" — yet no further appearances are described. No Google Business Profile or local directory presence is mentioned despite a quarterly in-person workshop near Temple Meads (A5). Instagram was abandoned after six months (F3) and £300 of LinkedIn ads produced zero bookings (F3). Visibility assets exist but are not working commercially.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: The one recorded borrowed-audience appearance delivered 4 clients × £1,800 (B2) = £7,200 from a single fortnight (F4). With no further appearances documented, this channel sits idle with that benchmark on the table. SEO and LinkedIn yield no bookings, so their attributable revenue is currently £0.

scores.evidence: The verbal positioning is genuinely sharp: (A2) "I coach software engineers who've just been made managers and are quietly drowning — I help them stop doing everyone else's job and start doing their own." The differentiator is specific and defensible: (E3) "I was an engineering manager for nine years — I've actually done the job, run the redundancy conversations, shipped late, been the one crying in the stairwell. Most leadership coaches came up through HR or L&D. Engineers can smell the difference inside ten minutes." However, this clarity is not translating commercially on the most active public channel: (B4) "LinkedIn posts get lovely comments and roughly zero bookings" — which means the message reads as interesting content, not a clear offer with a clear next step. The website's message is not described in the intake, so it cannot be assessed.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: LinkedIn currently produces (B4) "roughly zero bookings" despite regular posting — £0 attributed revenue from this active channel. If message sharpening converted even 1 booking/month from an already-maintained channel, that is 1 × £1,800 (B2) = £1,800/mo currently uncaptured.

scores.evidence: No booking mechanism, discovery call link, intake form, or explicit CTA is described anywhere in the intake. (B4): "Almost all of it is the 1:1 packages, and most of those come from referrals — ex-clients tipping off the next engineer who gets promoted at their old company" — conversion happens through warm personal introductions, not through any owned digital path. The newsletter converts but (F4) confirms the timeline: "people book after lurking for eight months." An eight-month consideration window for a £1,800 package strongly suggests there is no nudge shortening that path. LinkedIn and the website are listed as active channels (F1, B4) but no description is given of what a cold visitor is asked to do on arrival.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: 1,400 subscribers (F2) sit in a funnel with a stated 8-month average consideration period before booking (F4). No subscriber conversion rate was provided, so a precise monthly revenue figure cannot be honestly calculated. What is clear: every unnecessary month of delay per eventual client defers £1,800 (B2). A single added CTA costs nothing to test and nothing to build.

scores.evidence: (F2): "About 1,400 subscribers. I email most Tuesdays — skipped three weeks in May when the cohort work stacked up and felt guilty the entire time. Opens hover around 48%, which people tell me is good?" — 48% open rates are genuinely strong; this list is a real asset. But the newsletter is the only follow-up mechanism described. There is no mention of a welcome sequence for new subscribers, a follow-up process for enquiries that stall, or a structured ask to past clients. (F4) confirms that referrals are "probably 70% of bookings" yet they run on entirely unprompted goodwill — no referral-request email, no thank-you system, no 'here is exactly how to recommend me' note sent to people who completed a coaching package.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: Referrals = ~70% of 4 new clients/month (B3) = ~3 clients × £1,800 (B2) = ~£5,400/mo running on goodwill with no structured ask. A single referral-request email to past clients could yield 1 additional referral/month = £1,800/mo — derived only from B2 and the referral proportion stated in F4.

scores.evidence: (F4): "Referrals from past clients, full stop — probably 70% of bookings." The proof clearly exists and is compelling enough to drive most new business — but it is entirely private. No testimonials, published case studies, client outcome stories, or LinkedIn recommendations are mentioned in the intake. (F3) describes Instagram content that "got 11 likes, mostly from other coaches" — the intended audience of recently-promoted software engineers is not seeing evidence of results. (E3) provides strong credentials — nine years as an engineering manager — but credentials establish authority, not demonstrated client transformation. A cold visitor to the website or LinkedIn profile currently has no visible reason to trust.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: Without public proof, cold discovery paths (website, LinkedIn, SEO) convert at approximately £0 for this business — consistent with (B4) and (F3). Current new-client revenue = 4 (B3) × £1,800 (B2) = £7,200/mo, almost entirely gated behind the referral network. Growth is capped by that network's reach, not by market demand.

scores.evidence: (B1) shows a £3–10k price range — a wide spread that suggests either multiple unpackaged tiers or significant pricing variability at point of sale. (E4) confirms premium positioning. The core offer is conceptually clear (1:1 packages for engineers newly promoted to management), but (E2): "Individuals I mostly lose to doing nothing — they wait, hoping it clicks on its own" — this is both a visibility and an offer problem. When the only path to yes is a full 1:1 package, an already-overwhelmed new manager has an easy off-ramp: defer. No lower-commitment entry point — a diagnostic session, a defined short sprint, the quarterly in-person workshop positioned as a standalone — is described that could convert the undecided before they wait it out.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: The primary individual-prospect loss mechanism is inaction (E2), not named competitors. Each lost-to-inaction prospect represents an uncaptured £1,800 (B2). The volume of these lost prospects is not stated in the intake and cannot be invented — but inaction is identified as the dominant loss channel for individuals outside the referral network.

top_3_leaks: The borrowed-audience channel is sitting idle: one appearance on The Standup Log produced 4 clients × £1,800 = £7,200 and was never repeated. This is the highest-converting channel on record — more than six months of Instagram, £300 of LinkedIn ads, and a webinar combined — and it has not been systematically pursued.

The referral engine — ~70% of all bookings, worth approximately 3 clients × £1,800 = £5,400/mo — runs entirely on unprompted goodwill from past clients. There is no structured referral ask, no 'here is exactly how to recommend me' message, and no thank-you system that makes referring feel easy and obvious.

LinkedIn consumes real posting effort and produces (B4) 'roughly zero bookings' — the audience engaging with the content is predominantly other coaches, not software engineers who just got promoted. For a solo operator, time is the scarcest input; this channel is spending it without commercial return.
quick_wins: This week, email every past client individually — not a newsletter blast — with one sentence: 'I have a spot opening in [month] and if you know a software engineer who's just been made a manager and is struggling, I'd love an introduction.' Write their name at the top. No template. Twenty minutes, zero cost, and you will have done the structured referral ask for the first time.

Pitch three engineering or tech podcasts for a guest spot this week — find shows where recently-promoted engineering managers actually listen, not coaching shows. Use the A2 line as the pitch hook, verbatim: 'I coach software engineers who've just been made managers and are quietly drowning.' The Standup Log proved this audience converts; find three more rooms like it and send the emails.

Add one plain-text line to the bottom of next Tuesday's newsletter, above your sign-off: 'If this sounds like your week, I have one spot available — reply to this email or book a 20-minute call here: [link].' No design, no button, no image. Just the sentence. Track whether anyone clicks or replies before building anything more involved.
narrative_summary:
Priya, you have something most coaches don't: a positioning that's actually true. Nine years running engineering teams — being the one crying in the stairwell — is not a brand story, it's a fact, and the engineers you work with can tell the difference. The way you describe your work in the intake is cleaner and more specific than most businesses manage after years of trying to get it right.

What's already working: your referral engine is quietly exceptional. Seventy percent of bookings from past clients who care enough to recommend you is the strongest signal in this audit — it means the work lands. Your newsletter, with 48% open rates across 1,400 subscribers, is a genuine asset. And one podcast appearance outperformed six months of Instagram, three weeks of LinkedIn ads, and a webinar — combined.

Here's what's leaking: you are not doing deliberately the things that already work. The podcast taught you something important and then you didn't book another one. The referral channel runs on goodwill with no structured ask — one email to past clients this week could change that. Your newsletter nurtures people for eight months before they book, partly because there's no clear invitation to act sooner.

LinkedIn is where you're spending real time and collecting comments from other coaches. That's not nothing, but it isn't £1,800 either. The three quick wins this week are not about new channels or new strategies — they're about doing on purpose what your business already does by accident.
